title: Three answers: sat, unsat, unknown
objective: Say what sat, unsat and unknown each assert about one query, one encoding and one solver run, and what a deploy gate does with unknown.

choice.prompt: A deploy gate asks Z3 whether a new rule can overdraw any account. The answer is `unknown`. What is established?

options.text: No bug: no account can be overdrawn by the rule.
A bug: some account can be overdrawn by the new rule.
options.why: Only `sat` with a replayed model shows a violation.

options.text: Nothing: the gate blocks the rule until it is decided.
options.why: A gate that lets `unknown` through has no evidence at all.

options.text: Partly: the rule holds for each of the inputs Z3 tried.
options.why: Z3 reports no partial coverage. "Inputs tried" is a testing idea.

blocks.md: An answer is about one query, one encoding and one solver run. `sat` comes with a model you can replay. `unsat` means no input satisfies this query as encoded, if the solver is sound. `unknown` means Z3 did not decide, and the reason line says why.

blocks.direction: Query asserts: two whole numbers whose power is eight, with an exponent above one.

code.text:
from z3 import *
x, y = Ints('x y')
s = Solver()
s.add(x**y == 8, y > 1)
print(s.check())
print(s.reason_unknown())

options.why: `x = 2` and `y = 3` solve it, but an answer reports what Z3 decided, not the truth.
`x = 2` and `y = 3` solve it, so this misreads the constraint.
The reason line names the gap.

blocks.after: Z3 gave up, and the reason line says where: smt tactic failed to show goal to be sat/unsat (incomplete (theory arithmetic)) {{run:RUN-z3-unknown-pow}}. Yet `x = 2`, `y = 3` is a solution. `unknown` belongs to one query, not to a kind of arithmetic: a neighbouring query that fixes the base and the result, `2**x == y` with `x >= 0` and `y == 5`, gets a verdict {{run:RUN-z3-unknown-pow}}.

blocks.md: This query has no solution. It runs under a budget, `rlimit`, which counts solver work rather than seconds.
blocks.direction: Query asserts: three whole numbers above two whose cubes satisfy `x³ + y³ = z³`.

code.text:
from z3 import *
x, y, z = Ints('x y z')
s = Solver()
s.set('rlimit', 5000000)
s.add(x > 2, y > 2, z > 2, x*x*x + y*y*y == z*z*z)
print(s.check())
print(s.reason_unknown())

call.prompt: Z3 works until its budget ends. What does it say?

options.why: No solution exists, but Z3 has not shown that within the budget. Truth and verdict differ.
The reason, canceled, says the budget ran out {{run:RUN-z3-budget-pyodide}}.

blocks.after:
The reason is canceled {{run:RUN-z3-budget-pyodide}}. A larger budget could turn this `unknown` into a verdict, and a verdict at a stated `rlimit` can be run again.

Budgets come from `rlimit`, not from `timeout`. A `timeout` of two seconds never returned under Pyodide in a Node harness {{run:RUN-z3-budget-pyodide}}, nor in three desktop browsers {{run:RUN-phone-pyodide}}, so an outside limit has to stop the worker.

blocks.md: Where `unknown` guards enforcement, treat it as no. Amazon S3's Block Public Access analysis does: "To maintain soundness, we choose to fail closed: if the analysis result is unknown due to a time-out, we say the policy is not Trust Safe" (ESEC/FSE 2020, page 8).

choice.prompt: Which statement about one solver answer is true?

options.text: A `sat` on a violation query means the property holds.
options.why: `sat` comes with a model, and the model is a counterexample.

options.text: An `unknown` with the reason "canceled" means no counterexample exists.
options.why: It means the budget ran out before Z3 decided.

options.text: An `unsat` over `Int` also covers 64-bit integer code.
options.why: `Int` never overflows and 64-bit integers do, so the encoding differs.

options.text: An `unsat` is about its own query and encoding, if the solver is sound.
options.why: It is a statement about one query, one encoding and one solver run.

choice.prompt: A deploy gate checks a new rule, and the raw solver line is `unknown` with the reason "canceled" at the gate's budget {{run:RUN-z3-budget-pyodide}}. Which stamp does the gate record, and what does it do?

options.text: PROVED [P], no counterexample found: the gate allows the deploy.
options.why: `unknown` is no verdict, so nothing is proved.

options.text: UNKNOWN [?], canceled at the stated budget: the gate blocks the deploy.
options.why: With no evidence either way, a gate that guards enforcement fails closed.

options.text: REFUTED [R], a counterexample exists: the gate blocks the deploy.
options.why: A counterexample needs `sat` with a model that replays.

options.text: TESTED [T], no bug in the inputs tried: the gate allows the deploy.
options.why: A solver answer is not a test report, and `unknown` covers no inputs at all.

first_load.wire_basis: gzip, zlib level 5 (zlib 1.3.1), as W0-S08 found GitHub Pages sending it

ci_mapping.note: The gate asserts q_runner <= budget * (yardstick_runner / yardstick_here) / k, with k the reference-to-unthrottled ratio below and yardstick_here the unthrottled tier's JS yardstick; it needs the yardstick run on the runner.

notes: Question: how does Pyodide with the Z3 5.3.1 wheel behave on phones, from the instrument origin: load time, first-load size, memory, rlimit timing and cache persistence across sessions, and in browsers the timeout, unknown and Fixedpoint cases?
Answer on this machine: an emulation only. No phone was available, so every figure below that is not about bytes is a stand-in for a phone, and values.boot_budget is provisional.

First-load sizes are exact: the same bytes in every engine, as the browser reports them (Resource Timing or Content-Length) and as the server logged them. What is assumed is the host: gzip level 5 is what GitHub Pages sent for four small public files [X RUN-pglite-0511], and no file as large as pyodide.asm.wasm has been measured there.

rlimit is not a time budget. The same rlimit took a different wall time on the two query types, the second query ended sooner at 5e6 than at 1e6 once the SAT core cancelled itself, and the reason string changes with the stage that stopped (see checks[]).
The yardstick (a fixed xorshift loop in JavaScript and in WebAssembly, run in the worker) is the common scale between the emulated tiers and a phone: a device report carries the same loop.

WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes) did not settle in some Playwright WebKit sessions once Pyodide had loaded in the same worker; each session records the outcome (cpu.wasm_async_instantiate), and the yardstick times a module made by the synchronous constructors.

The planned fill (one message to the instrument service worker, which fetches the six files and answers) did not finish in Firefox on the 1.6 Mbit/s link: the browser stopped the worker about a minute in. A message to the worker every 15 s let the same fill finish in all three engines (docs/spikes/W0-S02.md section 4.8; verdict_lines, checks[] and observations.link carry the figures).

History of the link plan: its first attempt had no deadline on the fill, Firefox never answered at 1.6 Mbit/s, and that container was stopped by hand. The kit then gained the 180 s deadline, the check of the worker instance and the heartbeat variant, and the whole emulated run (every plan) was repeated on the changed kit. No figure of the first attempt is used here.
